Race against time

By: Annalise Lubbe | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
South Africa is banned from exporting racehorses directly to the overseas market. We witness the impact it has on the equine industry.

Unique Selling Point:
African Horse Sickness has brought the equine industry to it's knees. Horse Breeders, competitors and trainers are calling for change.

Summary:
It has been nine years since our last report on Carte Blanche and there has been no visible improvement in controlling African Horse Sickness or AHS. A vaccine for AHS was developed in 1957 and the only subsequent work that’s been done to improve the efficacy was in 1995. In 2006 Horse-owners asked whether a new vaccine would be developed. Onderstepoort Biological Products promised there would be one in five years. No new product has been made available.From a potentially R1 billion industry per annum the horse racing industry trickled down to R200 00 and more than 75 000 people lost their jobs. In a race against time South Africa is fighting to get the horse export ban imposed by the European Union lifted. AHS is a highly infectious and fatal disease and as many as 70% of horses die within one week of the infection. It is spread through tiny midges. When a midge bites an infected horse it carries the virus to a non-infected horse. The incubation period of AHS infection is 7 – 14 days but may be as short as two days. Symptoms include swelling above the eyes, sounds gurgling in their lungs as they battle to breathe and eventually a painful death for the animal.South Africa was banned from the international racehorse export market for many years. In a pro-active move a controlled AHS zone was established in 1997 in the Western Cape, historically known for few outbreaks. It consisted of a protection zone, a surveillance zone and a free zone spanning a total of 300km. The last stop for horses leaving South Africa was at the free zone at the Kenilworth Racecourse in Cape Town where horses would spend 21 days under quarantine. South Africa now had access to the European, Middle Eastern and Asian horseracing circuit provided we had no outbreaks in the safe zone. Continued outbreaks of AHS from 1999 to 2014 led to new restrictions by the EU. Besides the 21 days at Kenilworth, horses now had to spend 60 days in Mauritius and 30 days in the UK under quarantine.

Further information:
South Africa now had access to the European, Middle Eastern and Asian horseracing circuit provided we had no outbreaks in the safe zone. Unfortunately continued outbreaks of AHS from 1999 to 2014 led to new restrictions by the EU in the export of horses. Besides the 21 days at Kenilworth, horses now have to spend 60 days in Mauritius and 30 days in the UK under quarantine. This, says breeders like Mike de Kock is ludicrous as it severely hampers the performance of the racehorses.

De Kock, exporter and racehorse trainer, has been frustrated by the cumbersome process and will tell you that his horses shipped from South Africa have to spend a potential health threatening 147 days en rout to Dubai and elsewhere. This includes a 50 day residency period in Mauritius where they are locked in their stables from 4pm to 8h30 am with only an early morning feed and then 40 days in quarantine with a spell in the UK where severe climate changes have to be dealt with.
“The incubation period for African Horse Sickness is generally 14 days, he says, so if your horse is still alive after 21 days, it ain’t got horse sickness. Yet the Americans lock them up for 60 days. Even 90 days in Mauritius is over the top.

Stringent regulations over African Horse Sickness imposed by international governmental bodies, have isolated South Africa from easy movement of thoroughbreds and forced de Kock into a modern –day equivalent of Jules Verner’s hero in Gulliver’s Travel.

De Kock has won Group races on four continents, and after Vercingetorix took the recent Jebel Hatta in Dubai. He has trained the winner of at least one G1 race outside South Africa in eight of the last 12 years.

“Tonight we produced 3 high-class winners at a single international competition showing for the umpteenth time that we can compete with the world’s best yet the draconian protocols that prevent us from shipping bloodstock directly from South Africa to the various racing jurisdictions abroad, remain firmly in place with no light at the end of the tunnel”, he exclaimed. “Just imagine the heights we could reach if we were allowed to export our bloodstock within reasonable times, in line with the rest of the racing world. As it stands, our ability to compete on the racetrack and in the sales ring is limited, he says”

Horse racing breeders are pushing for change. Peter Gibson, CEO of Racing SA says “20 years later, with greater knowledge and improvement in science, we are worse off. The solution he feels is to create a full lock down station at Kennelworth; Improve technical and scientific capabilities beyond doubt; and improve the conditions for export. But unless Government and trade partners work together to develop a foolproof export protocol and negotiate with potential importing countries to accept their agreement, our local industry will continue suffering losses.

There is pressure from the equine industry to find a solution soon. The carrot at the end of the stick will be opening the doors for our local market to host the 2024 Olympics. But at this stage it is a pipe dream.

Conclusion:

The trade restrictions have resulted in a massive loss of investment for horseracing breeders, competitors and the dressage and endurance racing industry. The lengthy quarantine and residency requirements for horses exported via Mauritius are expensive and seriously jeopardise the physical and mental health of the horses, often leading to career threatening injuries.

In addition no overseas competitors will ever race in South Africa. Horses landing here are on a one-way ticket. South African breeders currently import about 300 horses from Australia every year for new bloodstock. On the flip side local breeders pay up to 3 times more to export their prize animals to buyers overseas due to the lengthy quarantine period and risk of injuries during their overstay.

Amongst the vets there is a general feeling that the very vaccine meant to protect the horses is making them sick. Data from a recent study shows that the use of polyvalent AHS virus-live attenuated vaccine can result in emergence and spread of virulent viruses to resident susceptible horses.

Some vets have lost faith in the Onderstepoort vaccine and have resorted to trying other products on the market. This pose a problem as only approved vaccines by DAFF and the World Organisation of Animal Health (OIE) is acceptable for the horse’s passport to allow travelling.

And finally, South Africa’s trading partners want a foolproof solution. A fully vector-protected lock-down quarantine station is necessary to facilitate the export of racehorses during the low vector-activity months. We investigate the reasons for the lack of pro-active steps from the government and speak to the horse owners and breeders about the impact the global ban has had on their business.

Press Release:


African Horse Sickness
African horse sickness is a highly infectious disease and it is wreaking havoc in South Africa’s multi-million rand horse-racing industry. As South Africa faces yet another
year of isolation from the world equine export market, horse breeders, trainers and competitors are all desperate for answers. Carte Blanche assesses the impact of this
deadly illness

Script:


Script: Race Against Time Duration: 10 minutes Date: 9 May 2017: Final

STUDIO LINK:
South Africa is banned from exporting racehorses directly to the overseas market due to a deadly disease we harbour. Stay with us as we investigate the impact African Horse Sickness has on the equine industry.
__________________________________________________________________________
SCRIPT:
Up audio: Commentator - J&B Met: “Smartcall in the middle then comes Legal Eagle towards the inside, it’s Smart Call with the head in front, it’s the fully that strikes the front but she is pulling clear in the closing stage. Smart Call wins the J&B Met from Legal Eagle, Captain America, Like The Lights, then came Paraphernalia and then Legislate”

Link: This is the starting point for horses that might eventually compete in the top races on the international stage but there is a major hurdle that they will have to overcome to make it to the likes of the Dubai World Cup and Royal Ascot.

V/O And this hurdle is African Horse Sickness. The disease is endemic to sub-saharan Africa and affects all breeds of horses. It is transmitted by tiny midges which become infected when feeding on other infected animals.

Up audio

V/O Peter Gibson of Racing South Africa works in partnership with the Department of Trade and Industry to promote our local bloodstock to the global market. Not an easy task as our international trading partners fear the spread of African Horse Sickness to their stables.

Derek Watts: Peter Is it possible to put a number on how much AHS has cost the racing industry alone?

Peter Gibson: CEO Racing South Africa: Derek it has affected the export primarily. We are exporting performance animals so it is across the board, whether it is polo, endurance or show jumping. We currently exporting we think on average basis about R250 million worth of horses. I think with a predictable fair export solution we could quadruple that to a billion rand industry.

Link: African Horse Sickness is a highly infectious and fatal disease and as many as 70% of the horses die within one week of the infection.

V/O African Horse Sickness or AHS was declared a state controlled disease in South Africa in 1984. Due to the seriousness of the disease, a global ban was imposed on the direct export of horses from South Africa. To overcome the hurdle a controlled area was established in the Western Cape where horses were free of the disease. The area consists of a small free zone, a protection zone and a surveillance zone spanning a 300 kilometre radius. This was accepted by the World Organisation for Animal Health and the EU countries provided there has been no outbreaks for a minimum period of 2 years. At the heart of the free zone is the Kenilworth quarantine station in Cape Town from where horses are shipped overseas. Gary Buhrmann is in control of animal health at the facility.

Dr. Gary Buhrmann: Chief State Veterinarian Boland: Department of Agriculture Western Cape:
This facility at Kenilworth is very unique in South Africa, it is one of the only ones of this standard, and basically we call it a vector protected quarantine, in other words insects cannot enter the quarantine.

V/O The Quarantine station is a sealed building and operates under positive pressure ventilation with a double door entry and exit.

Dr. Gary Buhrmann: So once the horses are within the facility no midges of any sort can actually penetrate it.

V/O By law all horses must be vaccinated but as much as 50% of our national herd, mostly from the rural areas, is unvaccinated. Through Illegal movements of these horses into the controlled area several outbreaks of AHS have prevented South Africa from direct exports.

Dr. Gary Buhrmann: Since the protocol has been in place with numerous zones we have had 5 outbreaks in the area. And what we determined through the research done at the equine research centre is that the last 4 outbreaks have been as a result of the live AHS vaccine.

V/O Through studies at The Equine Research Centre at the Onderstepoort Veterinary Faculty in Pretoria, Prof Alan Guthrie and his team found that the state produced vaccine from Onderstepoort Biological Products has in some instances been the cause of AHS.

Prof. Alan Guthrie: Director Equine Research Centre: The problem that we have with AHS is that you will get some horses which develop a reaction against it which in some cases is full blown AHS.

Derek Watts: So the vaccine can actually transmit the disease?

Alan Guthrie: It can transmit the disease and we have done some work which shows that the outbreaks in the Western Cape were due to viruses directly derived from the vaccine.

V/O With the threat of AHS spreading to uninfected countries the OIE increased the quarantine period for up to 70 days in isolation and up to 90 days residency before horses will be allowed on foreign soil.

Audio up

V/O Top trainer Mike de Kock who has had 3000 winners in his career has been frustrated by the cumbersome process of getting his prize animals into the international arena.

Mike de Kock: Racehorse Trainer: Derek, today it is a mission. We have an isolation period in the Cape for about 21 days, we then do 90 days in Mauritius, 40 of which are under quarantine supervision which means that the horses are locked up from 2 hours before sunset and only can exit 2 hours after sunrise. They do 90 days there then they do a 30 days residency in the EU either England or France and then they can go into the UAE.

Derek Watts: it’s an incredible saga?

MIke de Kock: It is and I mean we dealing with athletes in the end of the day and unfortunately in that time there isn’t a good amount of exercise for them. Some horses actually take a year to really come right.

V/O Candice is a shipping agent for people like Mike who have to get their horses overseas.

Candice Hobday: Shipping Agent: The economic tragedy of AHS is that it forces us to export the horses over a longer period of time, and on top of that you are looking at multiple flights. People don’t want to spend the money on transit and the time waiting to receive the horses.

Derek Watts: So Mike if you want to get him to Dubai to race what would it cost you?

MIke de Kock: it would cost you anything between 40 and 50 thousand dollars if everything goes right.

V/O Dr. Mpho Maja is in charge of horse export policies. Key to her role in monitoring and preventing the outbreak of AHS is regular vaccination of all horses. The vaccine is 60 years old.

Derek Watts: The vaccine was developed way back in 1957, has there been improvements made since then?

Dr. Mpho Maja: Director Animal Health: Department of Agriculture Forestry and Fisheries: I think the improvements that get made to the vaccine would be looking at the viruses that are circulating and upgrading it as and when the virus changes. I will be talking off if I said there had been great or significant improvements. I have little idea in that area.

Derek Watts: Doc you say that the vaccine is effective but some of our horses sit in quarantine for up to 160 days?

Dr. Mpho Maja: The vaccine is effective. The reason the horses stay in quarantine for that period is because the trade partner needs the assurance when they bring the horse into the country it is as free of the virus as we could possibly guarantee.

Link: This is the vaccine that has been used for decades but the search is on for a next generation vaccine that will be more effective in controlling the disease in Africa and be internationally acceptable trading partners.

V/O And the new vaccine will be from a killed virus and deemed much safer.

Prof. Alan Guthrie: The difference with a killed vaccine is what you do you take the virus and that it could never infect an animal. The problem is because it does not replicate in the animal the dose you have to give and the chemicals you have to add makes it a lot more expensive.

Derek Watts: So is it possible to say if you are getting closer to the launch of the new vaccine?

Prof Alan Guthrie: We are. We published a paper in 2009 and we have not managed to progress much beyond that concept because we have a little hurdle to get over which is funding for the next phase of the project which is estimated to be between 3 and 6 million Euro

Derek Watts: So that is what you need

Prof Alan Guthrie: Yes

V/O With limited government funds available a public private partnership might be the solution for the next phase in developing the new vaccine.

Derek Watts: What about developing a vaccine through a private partnership with a local company to be commercially viable?

Dr. Mpho Maja: That would be most welcome. If we could have a vaccine that works. Even motivate it to be registered.

Derek Watts: Do you think there has been enough drive from government and from the industry itself?

Mike de Kock: Look from our perspective there has been massive interest and push but as much as we drive and push we will get nowhere without the government. I believe we could employ many thousands more people, we have investment from overseas, starting up farms here to produce horses, shuttle stallions which will in turn upgrade our genetics. It’s massive.

V/O The global horse export market is worth US$4bn per year. South Africa’s market share is less than a quarter of 1%.

Derek Watts: Lifting the ban would mean huge financial growth for the equine industry, why has it not been a priority for the department?

Dr Mpho Maja: It is not that it is not a priority for government. The challenge is convincing the trade partners. But then that convincing seems to be having its shortcomings because everybody is so worried about importing the virus into their territory that it becomes a paper exercise that doesn’t seem to have an end.

V/O There is a desperate need for change; for government to enter high level negotiations with international trading partners; and for more funding to develop the new vaccine. Despite the many hurdles South Africa has bred some of the world’s top horses.

Peter Gibson: I will give you one good analogy of a top SA horse that went through the mill to get to Hong Kong where he won in fact. A lovely name JJ the Jetplane. He was at the time allowed to go directly into Europe. So he did a 40 day quarantine in Kenilworth he then flew to Europe, was isolated in the UK where he worked, he flew into Hong Kong a week before the race, got into the race and won a race worth 14 million Hong Kong Dollars. It proved, one that our horses are tough, secondly that we can compete against the best in the world and that we can earn significant prize money if given the chance.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
PROMOS:
UNMIXED TUESDAY BEFORE BROADCAST:
Teaser Promo (10sec): South Africa’s elite horses are effectively isolated from the rest of the world because of a deadly disease that has restricted the movement of our top performers.

Sound-up (4secs): Peter Gibson: We do believe that export and access to markets will allow significant investment into our equestrian industry.

Visuals: (30 seconds)
__________________________________________________________________________
ON DRIVE MIXED FOR BROADCAST:
Promo (10 seconds): V/O Horse breeders, trainers and competitors are desperate for change as they face isolation from the world’s horse export market due to African Horse Sickness.

Promo (15 seconds): Mike de Kock: We export maybe R200 million a year worth of horses. I believe personally it could get into the billions.
V/O South Africa has been restricted from the direct export of race horses globally due to the fear of African Horse Sickness.

Promo (15 seconds): V/O Quarantine, isolation, multiple flights, this is what our horses go through when competing on the international circuit.
Peter Gibson: It is a costly exercise, possibly $30 000 per horse. It is lengthy and the other major impact is on fitness level.

I confirm that all footage agreements have been signed and submitted via Jotform: No Music Cue Sheet Music Title Type Track Number Duration Publisher Composer Record/CD Number Echoes Instrumental 00:00:18 ART LIST Salt of the Sound N/A Echoes Instrumental 00:00:28 ART LIST Salt of the Sound N/A The tree of life Instrumental 00:00:42 ART LIST Marco Martini N/A The Doubt Instrumental 00:00:21 ART LIST Marco Martini N/A Discovery Instrumental 00:00:50 ART LIST Kevin Graham N/A TX Details Back references from Insert in Show: Title Author Last Updated 18 June 2017 - Carte Blanche HD Nikola Vrahimis 21 June 2017 Press Release: African Horse Sickness African horse sickness is a highly infectious disease and it is wreaking havoc in South Africa’s multi-million rand horse-racing industry. As South Africa faces yet another year of isolation from the world equine export market, horse breeders, trainers and competitors are all desperate for answers. Carte Blanche assesses the impact of this deadly illness Script: Script: Race Against Time Duration: 10 minutes Date: 9 May 2017: Final STUDIO LINK: South Africa is banned from exporting racehorses directly to the overseas market due to a deadly disease we harbour. Stay with us as we investigate the impact African Horse Sickness has on the equine industry. __________________________________________________________________________ SCRIPT: Up audio: Commentator - J&B Met: “Smartcall in the middle then comes Legal Eagle towards the inside, it’s Smart Call with the head in front, it’s the fully that strikes the front but she is pulling clear in the closing stage. Smart Call wins the J&B Met from Legal Eagle, Captain America, Like The Lights, then came Paraphernalia and then Legislate” Link: This is the starting point for horses that might eventually compete in the top races on the international stage but there is a major hurdle that they will have to overcome to make it to the likes of the Dubai World Cup and Royal Ascot. V/O And this hurdle is African Horse Sickness. The disease is endemic to sub-saharan Africa and affects all breeds of horses. It is transmitted by tiny midges which become infected when feeding on other infected animals. Up audio V/O Peter Gibson of Racing South Africa works in partnership with the Department of Trade and Industry to promote our local bloodstock to the global market. Not an easy task as our international trading partners fear the spread of African Horse Sickness to their stables. Derek Watts: Peter Is it possible to put a number on how much AHS has cost the racing industry alone? Peter Gibson: CEO Racing South Africa: Derek it has affected the export primarily. We are exporting performance animals so it is across the board, whether it is polo, endurance or show jumping. We currently exporting we think on average basis about R250 million worth of horses. I think with a predictable fair export solution we could quadruple that to a billion rand industry. Link: African Horse Sickness is a highly infectious and fatal disease and as many as 70% of the horses die within one week of the infection. V/O African Horse Sickness or AHS was declared a state controlled disease in South Africa in 1984. Due to the seriousness of the disease, a global ban was imposed on the direct export of horses from South Africa. To overcome the hurdle a controlled area was established in the Western Cape where horses were free of the disease. The area consists of a small free zone, a protection zone and a surveillance zone spanning a 300 kilometre radius. This was accepted by the World Organisation for Animal Health and the EU countries provided there has been no outbreaks for a minimum period of 2 years. At the heart of the free zone is the Kenilworth quarantine station in Cape Town from where horses are shipped overseas. Gary Buhrmann is in control of animal health at the facility. Dr. Gary Buhrmann: Chief State Veterinarian Boland: Department of Agriculture Western Cape: This facility at Kenilworth is very unique in South Africa, it is one of the only ones of this standard, and basically we call it a vector protected quarantine, in other words insects cannot enter the quarantine. V/O The Quarantine station is a sealed building and operates under positive pressure ventilation with a double door entry and exit. Dr. Gary Buhrmann: So once the horses are within the facility no midges of any sort can actually penetrate it. V/O By law all horses must be vaccinated but as much as 50% of our national herd, mostly from the rural areas, is unvaccinated. Through Illegal movements of these horses into the controlled area several outbreaks of AHS have prevented South Africa from direct exports. Dr. Gary Buhrmann: Since the protocol has been in place with numerous zones we have had 5 outbreaks in the area. And what we determined through the research done at the equine research centre is that the last 4 outbreaks have been as a result of the live AHS vaccine. V/O Through studies at The Equine Research Centre at the Onderstepoort Veterinary Faculty in Pretoria, Prof Alan Guthrie and his team found that the state produced vaccine from Onderstepoort Biological Products has in some instances been the cause of AHS. Prof. Alan Guthrie: Director Equine Research Centre: The problem that we have with AHS is that you will get some horses which develop a reaction against it which in some cases is full blown AHS. Derek Watts: So the vaccine can actually transmit the disease? Alan Guthrie: It can transmit the disease and we have done some work which shows that the outbreaks in the Western Cape were due to viruses directly derived from the vaccine. V/O With the threat of AHS spreading to uninfected countries the OIE increased the quarantine period for up to 70 days in isolation and up to 90 days residency before horses will be allowed on foreign soil. Audio up V/O Top trainer Mike de Kock who has had 3000 winners in his career has been frustrated by the cumbersome process of getting his prize animals into the international arena. Mike de Kock: Racehorse Trainer: Derek, today it is a mission. We have an isolation period in the Cape for about 21 days, we then do 90 days in Mauritius, 40 of which are under quarantine supervision which means that the horses are locked up from 2 hours before sunset and only can exit 2 hours after sunrise. They do 90 days there then they do a 30 days residency in the EU either England or France and then they can go into the UAE. Derek Watts: it’s an incredible saga? MIke de Kock: It is and I mean we dealing with athletes in the end of the day and unfortunately in that time there isn’t a good amount of exercise for them. Some horses actually take a year to really come right. V/O Candice is a shipping agent for people like Mike who have to get their horses overseas. Candice Hobday: Shipping Agent: The economic tragedy of AHS is that it forces us to export the horses over a longer period of time, and on top of that you are looking at multiple flights. People don’t want to spend the money on transit and the time waiting to receive the horses. Derek Watts: So Mike if you want to get him to Dubai to race what would it cost you? MIke de Kock: it would cost you anything between 40 and 50 thousand dollars if everything goes right. V/O Dr. Mpho Maja is in charge of horse export policies. Key to her role in monitoring and preventing the outbreak of AHS is regular vaccination of all horses. The vaccine is 60 years old. Derek Watts: The vaccine was developed way back in 1957, has there been improvements made since then? Dr. Mpho Maja: Director Animal Health: Department of Agriculture Forestry and Fisheries: I think the improvements that get made to the vaccine would be looking at the viruses that are circulating and upgrading it as and when the virus changes. I will be talking off if I said there had been great or significant improvements. I have little idea in that area. Derek Watts: Doc you say that the vaccine is effective but some of our horses sit in quarantine for up to 160 days? Dr. Mpho Maja: The vaccine is effective. The reason the horses stay in quarantine for that period is because the trade partner needs the assurance when they bring the horse into the country it is as free of the virus as we could possibly guarantee. Link: This is the vaccine that has been used for decades but the search is on for a next generation vaccine that will be more effective in controlling the disease in Africa and be internationally acceptable trading partners. V/O And the new vaccine will be from a killed virus and deemed much safer. Prof. Alan Guthrie: The difference with a killed vaccine is what you do you take the virus and that it could never infect an animal. The problem is because it does not replicate in the animal the dose you have to give and the chemicals you have to add makes it a lot more expensive. Derek Watts: So is it possible to say if you are getting closer to the launch of the new vaccine? Prof Alan Guthrie: We are. We published a paper in 2009 and we have not managed to progress much beyond that concept because we have a little hurdle to get over which is funding for the next phase of the project which is estimated to be between 3 and 6 million Euro Derek Watts: So that is what you need Prof Alan Guthrie: Yes V/O With limited government funds available a public private partnership might be the solution for the next phase in developing the new vaccine. Derek Watts: What about developing a vaccine through a private partnership with a local company to be commercially viable? Dr. Mpho Maja: That would be most welcome. If we could have a vaccine that works. Even motivate it to be registered. Derek Watts: Do you think there has been enough drive from government and from the industry itself? Mike de Kock: Look from our perspective there has been massive interest and push but as much as we drive and push we will get nowhere without the government. I believe we could employ many thousands more people, we have investment from overseas, starting up farms here to produce horses, shuttle stallions which will in turn upgrade our genetics. It’s massive. V/O The global horse export market is worth US$4bn per year. South Africa’s market share is less than a quarter of 1%. Derek Watts: Lifting the ban would mean huge financial growth for the equine industry, why has it not been a priority for the department? Dr Mpho Maja: It is not that it is not a priority for government. The challenge is convincing the trade partners. But then that convincing seems to be having its shortcomings because everybody is so worried about importing the virus into their territory that it becomes a paper exercise that doesn’t seem to have an end. V/O There is a desperate need for change; for government to enter high level negotiations with international trading partners; and for more funding to develop the new vaccine. Despite the many hurdles South Africa has bred some of the world’s top horses. Peter Gibson: I will give you one good analogy of a top SA horse that went through the mill to get to Hong Kong where he won in fact. A lovely name JJ the Jetplane. He was at the time allowed to go directly into Europe. So he did a 40 day quarantine in Kenilworth he then flew to Europe, was isolated in the UK where he worked, he flew into Hong Kong a week before the race, got into the race and won a race worth 14 million Hong Kong Dollars. It proved, one that our horses are tough, secondly that we can compete against the best in the world and that we can earn significant prize money if given the chance. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- PROMOS: UNMIXED TUESDAY BEFORE BROADCAST: Teaser Promo (10sec): South Africa’s elite horses are effectively isolated from the rest of the world because of a deadly disease that has restricted the movement of our top performers. Sound-up (4secs): Peter Gibson: We do believe that export and access to markets will allow significant investment into our equestrian industry. Visuals: (30 seconds) __________________________________________________________________________ ON DRIVE MIXED FOR BROADCAST: Promo (10 seconds): V/O Horse breeders, trainers and competitors are desperate for change as they face isolation from the world’s horse export market due to African Horse Sickness. Promo (15 seconds): Mike de Kock: We export maybe R200 million a year worth of horses. I believe personally it could get into the billions. V/O South Africa has been restricted from the direct export of race horses globally due to the fear of African Horse Sickness. Promo (15 seconds): V/O Quarantine, isolation, multiple flights, this is what our horses go through when competing on the international circuit. Peter Gibson: It is a costly exercise, possibly $30 000 per horse. It is lengthy and the other major impact is on fitness level. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): South Africa is banned from exporting racehorses directly to the overseas market. We witness the impact it has on the equine industry.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: African Horse Sickness has brought the equine industry to it's knees. Horse Breeders, competitors and trainers are calling for change.
metadata.Summary: It has been nine years since our last report on Carte Blanche and there has been no visible improvement in controlling African Horse Sickness or AHS. A vaccine for AHS was developed in 1957 and the only subsequent work that’s been done to improve the efficacy was in 1995. In 2006 Horse-owners asked whether a new vaccine would be developed. Onderstepoort Biological Products promised there would be one in five years. No new product has been made available.From a potentially R1 billion industry per annum the horse racing industry trickled down to R200 00 and more than 75 000 people lost their jobs. In a race against time South Africa is fighting to get the horse export ban imposed by the European Union lifted. AHS is a highly infectious and fatal disease and as many as 70% of horses die within one week of the infection. It is spread through tiny midges. When a midge bites an infected horse it carries the virus to a non-infected horse. The incubation period of AHS infection is 7 – 14 days but may be as short as two days. Symptoms include swelling above the eyes, sounds gurgling in their lungs as they battle to breathe and eventually a painful death for the animal.South Africa was banned from the international racehorse export market for many years. In a pro-active move a controlled AHS zone was established in 1997 in the Western Cape, historically known for few outbreaks. It consisted of a protection zone, a surveillance zone and a free zone spanning a total of 300km. The last stop for horses leaving South Africa was at the free zone at the Kenilworth Racecourse in Cape Town where horses would spend 21 days under quarantine. South Africa now had access to the European, Middle Eastern and Asian horseracing circuit provided we had no outbreaks in the safe zone. Continued outbreaks of AHS from 1999 to 2014 led to new restrictions by the EU. Besides the 21 days at Kenilworth, horses now had to spend 60 days in Mauritius and 30 days in the UK under quarantine.
metadata.Further information: South Africa now had access to the European, Middle Eastern and Asian horseracing circuit provided we had no outbreaks in the safe zone. Unfortunately continued outbreaks of AHS from 1999 to 2014 led to new restrictions by the EU in the export of horses. Besides the 21 days at Kenilworth, horses now have to spend 60 days in Mauritius and 30 days in the UK under quarantine. This, says breeders like Mike de Kock is ludicrous as it severely hampers the performance of the racehorses. De Kock, exporter and racehorse trainer, has been frustrated by the cumbersome process and will tell you that his horses shipped from South Africa have to spend a potential health threatening 147 days en rout to Dubai and elsewhere. This includes a 50 day residency period in Mauritius where they are locked in their stables from 4pm to 8h30 am with only an early morning feed and then 40 days in quarantine with a spell in the UK where severe climate changes have to be dealt with. “The incubation period for African Horse Sickness is generally 14 days, he says, so if your horse is still alive after 21 days, it ain’t got horse sickness. Yet the Americans lock them up for 60 days. Even 90 days in Mauritius is over the top. Stringent regulations over African Horse Sickness imposed by international governmental bodies, have isolated South Africa from easy movement of thoroughbreds and forced de Kock into a modern –day equivalent of Jules Verner’s hero in Gulliver’s Travel. De Kock has won Group races on four continents, and after Vercingetorix took the recent Jebel Hatta in Dubai. He has trained the winner of at least one G1 race outside South Africa in eight of the last 12 years. “Tonight we produced 3 high-class winners at a single international competition showing for the umpteenth time that we can compete with the world’s best yet the draconian protocols that prevent us from shipping bloodstock directly from South Africa to the various racing jurisdictions abroad, remain firmly in place with no light at the end of the tunnel”, he exclaimed. “Just imagine the heights we could reach if we were allowed to export our bloodstock within reasonable times, in line with the rest of the racing world. As it stands, our ability to compete on the racetrack and in the sales ring is limited, he says” Horse racing breeders are pushing for change. Peter Gibson, CEO of Racing SA says “20 years later, with greater knowledge and improvement in science, we are worse off. The solution he feels is to create a full lock down station at Kennelworth; Improve technical and scientific capabilities beyond doubt; and improve the conditions for export. But unless Government and trade partners work together to develop a foolproof export protocol and negotiate with potential importing countries to accept their agreement, our local industry will continue suffering losses. There is pressure from the equine industry to find a solution soon. The carrot at the end of the stick will be opening the doors for our local market to host the 2024 Olympics. But at this stage it is a pipe dream. Conclusion: The trade restrictions have resulted in a massive loss of investment for horseracing breeders, competitors and the dressage and endurance racing industry. The lengthy quarantine and residency requirements for horses exported via Mauritius are expensive and seriously jeopardise the physical and mental health of the horses, often leading to career threatening injuries. In addition no overseas competitors will ever race in South Africa. Horses landing here are on a one-way ticket. South African breeders currently import about 300 horses from Australia every year for new bloodstock. On the flip side local breeders pay up to 3 times more to export their prize animals to buyers overseas due to the lengthy quarantine period and risk of injuries during their overstay. Amongst the vets there is a general feeling that the very vaccine meant to protect the horses is making them sick. Data from a recent study shows that the use of polyvalent AHS virus-live attenuated vaccine can result in emergence and spread of virulent viruses to resident susceptible horses. Some vets have lost faith in the Onderstepoort vaccine and have resorted to trying other products on the market. This pose a problem as only approved vaccines by DAFF and the World Organisation of Animal Health (OIE) is acceptable for the horse’s passport to allow travelling. And finally, South Africa’s trading partners want a foolproof solution. A fully vector-protected lock-down quarantine station is necessary to facilitate the export of racehorses during the low vector-activity months. We investigate the reasons for the lack of pro-active steps from the government and speak to the horse owners and breeders about the impact the global ban has had on their business.
